analysis.one_liner: Guarantees health coverage to every U.S. resident through state purchasing cooperatives and regulated private health plans.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 102nd Congress with zero cosponsors, the bill never got a committee hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would entitle every U.S. resident to a standard package of health coverage, purchased through state-run nonprofit insurance purchasing cooperatives from regulated private "accountable health plans." Plans could not deny or price coverage based on health status, preexisting-condition exclusions would be capped, and employers would have to enroll workers or pay a penalty on health spending above the plan cost. A new federal board would set benefits, collect outcome data, and manage a national health budget. It was referred to committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 35 million-plus uninsured Americans of the early 1990s, people with preexisting conditions who could be denied or priced out of coverage, and workers changing or losing jobs who would gain portable, continuous coverage with only a limited preexisting-condition waiting period. Low-income people and small-business employees would get premium and cost-sharing assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen, national, or lawful resident alien would be entitled to coverage purchased through a state health insurance purchasing cooperative, with automatic enrollment at birth or upon immigration.

Health plans could not deny, limit, or condition coverage based on health status, claims experience, or medical history, and preexisting-condition exclusions could last no more than six months, reduced month-for-month by prior continuous coverage.
Plans would have to charge standard premiums using adjusted community rating based only on age, gender, and geography, ending the practice of charging sick individuals more within a purchasing area.

The National Health Care Board would establish low-income premium and cost-sharing assistance and an assistance program for small-business employees, and states would have to keep coverage flowing to people who move between states.

Plans would have to cover a uniform set of effective benefits set annually by the Board, meet solvency standards, provide grievance procedures, and restrict physician incentive plans that reward limiting care.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would be obligated to enroll employees in accountable health plans and would owe a civil penalty equal to 34 percent of any health plan expenses not paid through an accountable health plan or the cooperative; states, which must raise revenue for their share of the national health budget; and federal taxpayers, who would fund the federal contribution determined by the Board. Private insurers and HMOs would lose the ability to underwrite based on health status.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes state health insurance purchasing cooperatives the sole lawful mechanism for buying coverage and repeals the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, locking private managed-care plans in as the permanent channel for what would be a universal entitlement rather than offering a simpler public option.

One year after enactment, states could no longer require richer benefits than the federal uniform package, nor restrict network plans, utilization review, or provider limits, preempting state consumer-protection laws in the name of standardization.

The bill exempts from antitrust law any hospital agreement to share expensive services or technology, subject to Board approval, easing limits on hospital combinations at a time of rising hospital prices.

An 11-member appointed National Health Care Board would set benefits, budgets, and funding mechanisms, with its actions taking effect unless Congress affirmatively passed a joint resolution to block them, shifting major policy choices to an unelected body.

Employers would face new obligations and a 34 percent penalty on health expenses outside the accountable health plan system, a real cost that supporters of universal coverage would have to defend against the benefit of guaranteed enrollment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — guaranteed coverage that cannot be denied or priced by health status — is substantial and was the central goal of the early-1990s reform debate. But the design leans heavily on private managed competition: it entrenches insurers as the mandatory middlemen, preempts state consumer protections, grants sweeping power to an appointed board, and leaves the financing mechanism to be worked out later. A supporter of single-payer-style reform could honestly object that the bill buys universal coverage at the price of permanently embedding the insurance industry and managed-care restrictions in federal law.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the closing weeks of the 102nd Congress with no cosponsors, it was referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Bingaman introduced the 21st Century Health Care Act in the Senate on October 1, 1992, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No cosponsors signed on to the bill.
The committee took no further action; the bill's entire recorded history is introduction and referral, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed position because the bill never moved, but the status quo was preserved: private insurers kept their ability to underwrite and deny coverage, employers kept existing health arrangements, and no new federal health bureaucracy or mandate was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the health status quo

for.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and had it referred to committee.

against.name: Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee without action when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no organized support or opposition on either side.

industries.note: The bill forces every resident to obtain coverage through private accountable health plans purchased via state cooperatives, guaranteeing insurers a universal customer base and repealing the separate federal employees program — while simultaneously stripping their ability to deny or rate by health status. It entrenches the industry as the permanent channel for universal coverage rather than replacing it.

Employers would be obligated to enroll employees in plans and would owe a penalty equal to 34 percent of health plan expenses not paid through an accountable health plan, making employer spending the bill's main funding lever.

Title IV exempts hospital agreements to share expensive services and technology from antitrust law with Board approval, loosening competition limits on hospital consolidation in an era of rising hospital prices.

States would have to establish purchasing cooperatives and raise revenue for their share of a federal health budget, but would lose authority to set their own benefit mandates or restrict managed-care practices.
